A member covers a path when it equals the path or is a prefix of it ending at a '/' boundary; the absent cone covers everything (dense operation).
column4: an empty cone cannot be built, as in zit: at least one inclusion is required

column3: A worktree cone is checkout-local state recorded with the checkout's other local records; it is not an artifact, does not synchronize, and affects no artifact's bytes or name.
A cone may be widened or narrowed at any time.

The canonical serialization marks a cone carrying members of other kinds with a distinct version, and an implementation that does not understand a version refuses the cone rather than reading it as path members.
Refusal of a store cone is policy loss: the store heals toward dense.
Members are normalized through the worktree-path validation applied to tracked paths: no dot or dot-dot components, no empty components, no reserved roots.
A member covered by another member of the same polarity with no opposite-polarity member between them is removed, and the normalized cone is what classification uses.
At least 64 members are supported, and 255 should be.
Coverage is decided by the longest member of either polarity that covers the path, which is order-independent, so the canonical sorted serialization and the digest do not depend on input order.
Polarity may alternate along a nesting chain: a subtree excluded from an inclusion may contain a deeper re-inclusion.
A member whose nearest covering member has the same polarity is redundant and is removed.
An exclusion that no inclusion covers is a dead rule and is refused.
One path carried with both polarities is a contradiction and is refused.
A key range wholly inside an inclusion and outside every exclusion classifies as before; a range an exclusion intersects is classified per file, at no cost to correctness.
Members are literal path prefixes; glob and pattern members are not part of the mechanism.
A member names a directory subtree or a single file with equal standing.
A metacharacter in a member is a literal character of the path: it is never expanded, and the member may be refused.
Amending a cone by wholesale replacement and by member addition or removal are equivalent, and the incremental form should be offered.
Widening fetches what the cone newly covers (the policy form of demand fetch).
column4: over a dense store widening materializes from the store; demand fetch over a sparse store is Appendix A step 4

column3: Narrowing dematerializes and leaves reclamation to explicit compaction.
The sparse worktree is available to any conforming repository, with flat or tree-structured manifests.
A checkout operation given a cone materializes exactly the covered files.
The managed-file record covers only in-cone files.
column4: the strict three-physical-row fixture passes on the private-marker implementation; marker transitions, legacy unstamped undo refusal and cone-stamped undo images are reviewed; durable crash recovery of the marker remains unverified

column3: Status, untracked-file listing and bulk tracking operate within the cone; an uncovered on-disk path is neither reported as untracked nor eligible for tracking.
A request to track a path outside the cone is refused, and the refusal names the cone as the reason; a diagnostic that reports a missing file or alleges damage does not conform.
All file-set enumeration flows through the shared enumeration interface with the cone applied there as a range predicate, never filtered at individual call sites.
A commit from a sparse worktree produces a check-in whose file set is the in-cone files as observed in the worktree and the baseline's out-of-cone entries carried unchanged.
For flat manifests the baseline's out-of-cone F cards are copied byte-verbatim, merged in sorted order with the in-cone F cards.

Tree commits produce full canonical construction under the requested k; opaque reuse requires compatible partition evidence bound to the immutable parent, rules and k or verification from needed descriptors and entries. The structural affected range includes MAX-cut shifts, final-small-group merges and propagation at every height; necessary absent nodes are fetched or cause explicit refusal without a partial check-in.
The result is an ordinary check-in: a reader cannot detect that it was committed sparsely, and no new artifact form is introduced.
A sparse-worktree commit over a dense store may compute the R card by reading out-of-cone content from the store.
A commit over a sparse store omits the R card.
Verifiers do not treat an absent R card as damage.
A verifier checking a present R card during a sparse materialization computes the aggregate over the dense enumeration, reading out-of-cone content from the store.
column4: materialization verifies no R card; manifest.VerifyRCard, which every commit runs, always aggregates the dense enumeration

column3: A verifier over a sparse store skips R verification rather than report disagreement.
Over a dense store, merge, update and revert apply changes to out-of-cone files to the record without materializing them.
column4: record-only merge and conflict, update keeping the pending merge, partial-commit queue handling, mode-only revert and undo after cone changes are reviewed against fossil; revert of a record-only change has no conformance case and stash apply on a sparse checkout is untested

column3: The count of out-of-cone changes applied should be reported.
Read operations on an uncovered path over a dense store read the store: the cone governs materialization, not readability.
A sparse store requires tree manifests for the segment it elides; a flat segment may elide only its content blobs and holds its manifests densely.

A store sparse at a cone holds every manifest, every in-cone sub-manifest node and every blob an in-cone F card names, and every non-manifest structural artifact densely. Out-of-cone nodes and blobs MAY be absent as elided phantoms; already-held or demand-fetched payloads need not be discarded.
Transit phantoms, shunned artifacts and elided phantoms are distinguished; synchronization does not spontaneously request an elided phantom, whose absence is healthy.
Elision is computed from the cone, not stored on the phantom: reclassification on cone change is recomputation, and losing the store cone should reclassify every elided phantom as a transit phantom.
Verification reports a store complete within its cone as healthy, reports elision counts distinctly from damage, and reports transit phantoms and damaged in-cone artifacts as for a dense store.

A commit may reference elided subtrees proved identical to canonical construction by hash without possession; nodes required for boundary propagation or partition validation are fetched or cause explicit refusal. Pushing a canonically valid check-in is sound.
A server should refuse to be a clone origin for cones it does not cover, unless configured as a partial mirror, with one error card and no content.
column4: internal handler refusal and override are tested; public partial-mirror configuration remains pending

column3: A client treats a clone-round reply that carries an error card and no clone progress as fatal.
Widening reclassifies the newly covered elided phantoms as transit phantoms and fetches them.

Narrowing does not by itself delete held content; only explicit compaction deletes, dropping artifacts both out-of-cone and unreferenced by any spine, through the store-rewrite machinery and its locks.
column4: internal file and limited interior-node compaction are tested; provenance-bearing leaves and nonterminal paths remain held, and the public entry point is pending

column3: The flat prefix of a hybrid history holds its manifests densely; its content blobs may be elided by F-card classification.
A cone-scoped pull or clone adds one pragma cone card per inclusion member, encoded exactly as an F-card filename, and one pragma cone-not card per exclusion.
For check-in content a cone-scoped request asks for spines, in-cone sub-manifest nodes and in-cone blobs, and neither expects nor requests the remainder.
column4: aware clone and pull are tested; provenance-bearing outside nodes are conservatively retained rather than fully elided

column3: A cone-aware server walks each check-in's tree descending only nodes whose key range intersects the cone, emits the spine, the in-cone nodes and blobs, and bounds the per-round walk as a dense clone bounds its batches.
column4: current raw provenance discovery scans the whole held store per request; bounded selective preprocessing is unresolved

column3: A cone-aware server does not serve a delta whose base is outside the keep set it computed for the request; it serves that artifact in full form.
A recipient treats a phantom that a retained delta names as its source as a transit phantom whatever its cone classification.
Against a cone-ignorant server the requester filters locally: it stores in-cone artifacts, records elided phantoms for the remainder and reports the counts.
column4: ignored-pragma clone and pull filtering and counts are tested; provenance-bearing outside nodes remain held

column3: A cone-aware server should advertise the capability.
An operation over a sparse store that crosses the cone resolves elided phantoms by a targeted request or by the policy form, which is recommended for lasting intent.
column4: internal explicit-peer policy fetch is tested; public operations and saved-peer integration remain pending

column3: With no configured peer the operation refuses, and the diagnostic names the class (the count elided by the cone and the absence of a peer), never missing or corrupt.
column4: internal explicit-peer refusal and cancellation are tested; public operations and saved-peer integration remain pending

column3: Derived caches are cone-independent: their keys do not incorporate the cone.
The member count and member length of a cone are bounded with the same limits applied to F-card filenames.
The server-side tree walk on cone requests carries the depth and visited-node bounds of single-name lookup.
